subject: Climate & Environment
title: Deforestation and Carbon Release
description: One-minute skill: Deforestation and Carbon Release.

hook.text: A single large tree stores about one ton of CO₂ over its lifetime.

buildup.text: Forests absorb roughly 30% of human CO₂ emissions each year. They are Earth's lungs.

discovery.text: When trees are cut or burned, all that stored carbon goes back into the atmosphere.

twist.text: Tropical deforestation releases more CO₂ than the entire European Union each year.

climax.text: Cleared land absorbs less CO₂, so the planet loses a carbon sink and gains a source.

punchline.text: Every fallen tree is a carbon vault broken open.

quiz.question: What fraction of human CO₂ emissions do forests absorb?

details.summary: Deforestation accounts for roughly 10 percent of global CO2 emissions, releasing stored carbon when trees are burned or decompose. Tropical forests hold the most carbon, and their conversion to farmland creates a double loss by removing both carbon sinks and future absorption capacity.
details.whyItMatters: Stopping deforestation is one of the cheapest and fastest ways to cut emissions. Forests absorb CO2 only while standing; once felled, their carbon returns to the atmosphere.
takeaways: Deforestation contributes roughly 10 percent of global CO2 emissions
Tropical forests store the most carbon per hectare
Protecting forests preserves both stored carbon and future absorption

faq.question: How much CO2 does deforestation release each year?
faq.answer: Tropical deforestation and land-use change release roughly 4 to 5 billion tons of CO2 per year. This makes it the third-largest emission source after energy and industry, comparable to the total output of the European Union.

faq.question: Can planting new trees offset deforestation emissions?
faq.answer: New plantings help but take decades to store significant carbon. Old-growth forests contain far more carbon than young trees and support irreplaceable biodiversity. Preventing deforestation is far more effective than planting to compensate for loss.
